title: The Law of Large Numbers
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For independent identically distributed variables with finite mean μ, the sample average converges to μ — in probability (weak law) and almost surely (strong law).
short: Averaging many independent trials settles down to the true mean, and the strong law says it does so on almost every outcome.
long: The weak and strong laws assert different modes of convergence, and the distinction matters. The weak law says the chance of a noticeable gap between average and mean tends to zero; the strong law says that with probability one the entire infinite sequence of averages eventually stays within any chosen tolerance. Both need only a finite first moment for independent identically distributed variables, but the strong law is genuinely stronger: it speaks of a single random outcome rather than of probabilities at each finite n.
proof: Write \bar X_n-\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu). With finite variance, Chebyshev gives P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(X_1)/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0; truncation extends the weak law to a finite first moment. Kolmogorov's inequality or martingale convergence upgrades this to almost-sure convergence in the strong law.
consequence: It justifies long-run frequencies as probabilities, underpins Monte Carlo estimation, and explains why casinos and insurers can rely on averaging over many independent trials.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Standardized sums of independent identically distributed variables with finite variance converge in distribution to the standard normal bell curve.
short: Add enough small independent effects and their standardized sum looks Gaussian, whatever the individual distribution was.
long: The theorem is remarkable because it demands almost nothing about the shape of the underlying distribution: a single finite variance is enough for the normal law to emerge. After standardising by n and σ, all that survives in the limit is the quadratic term of the characteristic function near zero. This is why measurement errors, sums of small independent effects and noise built from many sources look bell-shaped even when no individual source is normal.
proof: Let \varphi(t)=\mathbb E[e^{it(X-\mu)}]; Taylor expansion gives \varphi(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2). The characteristic function of (S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n) is \varphi(t/(\sigma\sqrt n))^n\to e^{-t^2/2}, the characteristic function of \mathcal N(0,1); Lévy continuity converts this into convergence in distribution.
consequence: It explains why normal error models appear everywhere, justifies approximate confidence intervals and tests, and makes the bell curve the universal attractor of accumulated noise.

title: Bayes' Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If B has positive probability, the probability of A given B is the probability of B given A times the probability of A, divided by the probability of B.
short: It flips a conditional probability around, turning a likelihood into a posterior belief by way of a prior.
long: Bayes' theorem is a tautology about conditional probability, yet it reorganises how one reasons under uncertainty. It converts a likelihood — how expected the evidence is if a hypothesis holds — into a posterior belief by multiplying by a prior and dividing by the overall chance of the evidence. The denominator is often the hard part, and it is what makes rare conditions so easy to misjudge.
proof: Since A\cap B=B\cap A, we have P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B); expanding P(B) by the law of total probability gives the usual normalising denominator.
consequence: It turns diagnostic testing into arithmetic: a highly accurate test can still give a low posterior probability when the condition is rare, which is the base-rate fallacy.

title: The Law of the Unconscious Statistician
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The expectation of g(X) can be computed by integrating g against the distribution of X alone; there is no need to find the distribution of g(X).
short: To average a function of a random variable, weight the function by the original density and skip the change of variables.
long: A naive approach to E[g(X)] would find the density of g(X) by changing variables, which can be messy when g folds several values of X onto one. The law of the unconscious statistician bypasses that step entirely: the expectation is an integral over the original variable weighted by its density. It works for any measurable g for which the integral exists, and the same idea underlies importance sampling and the delta method.
proof: For discrete X, E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)P(X=x) is immediate from the definition. For continuous X with density f, approximate g by simple functions; from P(g(X)\in B)=P(X\in g^{-1}(B)) one gets E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx.
consequence: It lets statisticians compute moments of transformations — squares, logs, exponentials — without deriving new densities, and it is the workhorse behind the delta method.

title: The Birthday Problem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: In a room of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is already greater than one half.
short: Counting pairs instead of people reveals why a coincidence that feels rare is actually the likely outcome.
long: The surprising part is not the calculation but the number: 23. Computing the complement is easier than tracking coincidences directly — multiply the chances that each successive birthday is new. The result crosses one half at 23 people and exceeds 99% by 57. Real birthdays are not quite uniform, and that unevenness tends only to make collisions more likely.
proof: The probability all 23 birthdays differ is (365/365)(364/365)\cdots(343/365)=\prod_{k=0}^{22}(1-k/365)\approx0.493; its complement is about 0.507. The same product with 57 factors drops below 0.01.
consequence: It is a classic lesson that uniform-looking coincidence is far more likely than intuition suggests, and it is used in hashing, cryptography and the analysis of random assignments.

title: The Monty Hall Problem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: After the host reveals a goat, switching doors wins the car with probability 2/3 rather than 1/2 — provided the host always reveals a goat deliberately.
short: The host's knowledge, not the mere sight of a goat, is what doubles the value of switching.
long: The puzzle is a contest over conditioning, not over doors. If the initial choice is wrong — probability 2/3 — the host has no freedom and must open the only remaining goat door, so switching wins. If the initial choice is right, switching loses. The famous 1/2 answer comes from assuming the host opens a door at random without knowing the location, or from failing to specify the protocol at all.
proof: Initially the car is behind the chosen door with probability 1/3 and behind one of the other two with probability 2/3. A host who knows the location and must reveal a goat concentrates that 2/3 on the single unopened door. If instead the host picks a door at random and happens to reveal a goat, the posterior is 1/2.
consequence: It is a standard test of conditional reasoning and a warning that the answer depends on the protocol of the information revealed, not just on the information itself.

title: The Borel–Cantelli Lemma
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If the probabilities of a sequence of events sum to a finite number, then almost surely only finitely many of those events occur.
short: A summable sequence of chances cannot keep happening forever, and no independence is needed to prove it.
long: The lemma has two halves with different hypotheses, and confusing them is a common error. Convergence of the sum forces only finitely many events to occur, with no independence assumption whatsoever. The converse — that a divergent sum gives infinitely many occurrences — needs independence, or a weakening of it. This asymmetry is what makes the lemma so useful: the easy direction is precisely the one that proves almost-sure results.
proof: For every m, P(\limsup E_n)\le P(\bigcup_{n\ge m}E_n)\le\sum_{n\ge m}P(E_n), and the tail sum tends to zero. The converse direction instead uses independence and P(\bigcup_{n=m}^{N}E_n)\ge1-\exp(-\sum_{n=m}^{N}P(E_n)).
consequence: It gives a clean criterion for infinitely many events, powers almost-sure convergence proofs, and lies behind the infinite-monkey result.

title: The Optional Stopping Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a martingale, the expected value at a bounded stopping time equals its initial value: no betting system can create expected profit.
short: A fair game stays fair when you quit according to a rule that does not depend on the future.
long: A martingale models a fair game: given everything seen so far, the next value has conditional expectation equal to the present. Optional stopping asks whether a cleverly chosen quitting rule can extract profit from such a game. The theorem says no, provided the stopping time is bounded or the martingale is uniformly integrable. Dropping those hypotheses produces famous counterexamples, including doubling strategies stopped at an unbounded time.
proof: For a bounded stopping time T\le N, write M_T-M_0=\sum_{k=1}^{N}(M_k-M_{k-1})1_{\{T\ge k\}}; the indicator is measurable before time k, so each term has expectation zero by the martingale property. Uniform integrability extends the identity beyond bounded T.
consequence: It validates the martingale model of fair games and clarifies why betting more after losses cannot beat a fair game under realistic stopping rules.

title: Chebyshev's Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: No matter the distribution, the probability of straying more than k standard deviations from the mean is at most 1/k².
short: Two moments are enough to bound any tail, whatever shape the distribution has.
long: Markov's inequality applied to the squared deviation turns into Chebyshev with one line, and the result is striking for how little it assumes. No shape, no symmetry and no higher moments are required — only a finite variance. The bound is usually loose, but its universality makes it the standard tool for proving convergence and for distribution-free guarantees.
proof: Apply Markov's inequality to the nonnegative variable (X-\mu)^2 with threshold a=k^2\sigma^2: P((X-\mu)^2\ge k^2\sigma^2)\le\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^2]/(k^2\sigma^2)=1/k^2.
consequence: It applies to every distribution with finite variance, giving distribution-free quality-control bounds and a short proof of the weak law of large numbers.

title: The Coupon Collector's Problem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: To collect every one of n coupon types you need about n ln n draws — the final few types dominate the wait.
short: The last missing coupon is the expensive one: expectation grows like n log n, not n.
long: The first few coupons arrive quickly, but the last missing type can take a very long time to appear. Decompose the total waiting time into independent geometric pieces: once k types are in hand, each new draw is a winner with probability (n - k)/n. Summing the mean waiting times gives n times the n-th harmonic number. The n log n growth, rather than a mere n, is the lesson.
proof: With k types collected the chance of a new one is (n-k)/n, so the mean additional wait is n/(n-k). Summing k=0,\dots,n-1 gives n\sum_{j=1}^{n}1/j=nH_n, and H_n=\ln n+\gamma+o(1).
consequence: It models waiting times in hashing, network polling and DNA sequencing, and shows that the tail of a collection process costs far more than its bulk.

title: The Gambler's Ruin Problem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A gambler facing an infinitely rich opponent in a fair game is ruined almost surely; against a finite bank, the win probability equals their share of the total capital.
latex: P_i(\text{reach }N\text{ before }0)=\frac{i}{N},\qquad P_i(\text{ruin vs. infinite bank})=1
short: Even a fair game is fatal against an unlimited opponent, because zero is absorbing and infinity is not.
long: The fair random walk on {0,…,N} is a harmonic-function problem: the winning probability at each interior state is the average of its neighbours, with boundary values 0 and 1. The only solution is the straight line i/N. Letting N grow without bound gives the classical ruin result — against an infinitely rich opponent the walk hits zero eventually with probability one. A bias in the gambler's favour is required to make ever hitting zero less than certain.
proof: Let p_i be the chance of reaching N before 0 from i. Then p_i=(p_{i-1}+p_{i+1})/2 with p_0=0, p_N=1, so p_i=i/N by linearity. On the half-line {0,1,2,…} the recurrence with p_i\to0 at infinity forces p_i=0, i.e. certain ruin.
consequence: It quantifies ruin risk for gamblers and insurers, and is the prototype for hitting probabilities of random walks and Brownian motion.

title: Sums of Independent Normals Are Normal
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A linear combination of independent normal random variables is itself normal, with mean and variance obtained by the same linear rules.
short: Gaussian noise is closed under linear combinations: means add linearly and variances add quadratically.
long: Normal variables are closed under affine combinations: independence makes the variances add while the means combine linearly. This stability is rare — most distributions are not reproduced by summing their own kind — and it is why the Gaussian family is so convenient to work with. Together with the central limit theorem it explains why the normal distribution appears both as an exact model and as a universal approximation.
proof: The characteristic function of \sum_i a_iX_i is \prod_i\exp(i t a_i\mu_i-\tfrac12 t^2a_i^2\sigma_i^2)=\exp(i t\sum_i a_i\mu_i-\tfrac12 t^2\sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2), which is the characteristic function of the stated normal; uniqueness of characteristic functions finishes the proof.
consequence: It makes Gaussian noise closed under linear operations — the reason least squares, Kalman filters and the central limit theorem all produce normal answers.
